claims.text: The target protective coating has an FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy microstructure.
Controlled in-flight oxidation during HVOF deposition can generate nanoscale oxide dispersoids in the coating.
The controlled oxidation process will produce a uniform dispersoid distribution.
The oxide dispersoids will occur both along grain boundaries and within the matrix.
Nanoscale oxide dispersoids act as pinning points for dislocations.
Dispersoid pinning inhibits dislocation glide during prolonged loading.
Dispersoid pinning inhibits dislocation climb during prolonged loading.
Inhibiting dislocation motion reduces creep rate and progressive plastic deformation.
Fine, dense dispersed second phases can contribute to strengthening in a dual-phase FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy.
A conventional HVOF coating without controlled in-flight oxidation lacks a uniform population of nanoscale oxide dispersoids.
Under identical creep-test conditions, the oxide-tailored coating will accumulate less creep strain than the baseline coating.
The oxide-tailored coating will exhibit microstructural evidence of dislocation pinning.
The creep-resistance benefit will persist under continuous service-level loading at temperatures dominated by dislocation-mediated creep.
The magnitude of creep-rate reduction may vary with HVOF processing parameters and deposition environment.
The proposed controlled comparison uses otherwise identical HVOF coatings with and without intentional in-flight oxidation.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in creep strain together with evidence of effective dislocation pinning would falsify the proposed mechanism.
